title: Sort Array by Increasing Frequency
summary: Sort the values by how often they occur, least frequent first; values with the same frequency go in decreasing order.
statement:
Sort `nums` so that values that occur less often come first. If two values occur equally often, put the larger value first.

Return the sorted array (each value keeps all of its copies).
hints: First count how often each value occurs.
Sort with a custom comparator: by frequency ascending, then by value descending.
Java cannot sort an int[] with a comparator, so box it (Integer[] or a stream), or sort the distinct values and write each one out frequency times.

title: Sort an Array
summary: Sort the array in ascending order without a built-in sort, in O(n log n) time (merge sort, heap sort or a randomised quick sort).
statement:
Sort `nums` in ascending order and return it, without using any built-in sort function.

Your algorithm must run in O(n log n) time; the large test punishes quadratic sorts.
hints: Merge sort always runs in O(n log n): split the array in half, sort each half, and merge them.
Quick sort is O(n log n) on average, but a fixed pivot degrades to O(n²) on sorted input or many duplicates. Pick a random pivot and use three-way partitioning.
Heap sort works in place in O(n log n). With values in a small range, counting sort is O(n + range).

title: Largest Number
summary: Arrange the non-negative integers so their concatenation is the largest possible number, returned as a string (no leading zeros except "0").
statement:
Arrange the non-negative integers in `nums` in an order such that, written one after another, they form the largest possible number. Return it as a string, because it may be very large.

The result has no leading zeros, except that an answer of zero is `"0"`.
hints: Sorting by numeric value or by plain string order both fail: "3" vs "30" vs "34".
Compare two numbers a and b by which concatenation is bigger: a + b or b + a (as strings).
Sort with that comparator and join. If the first string is "0", every value was 0, so return "0".

title: H-Index
summary: citations[i] is the citation count of paper i. Return the largest h such that at least h papers have h or more citations each.
statement:
`citations[i]` is the number of citations of a researcher's `i`-th paper. The h-index is the largest `h` such that the researcher has at least `h` papers that each have at least `h` citations.

Return the h-index.
hints: Sort the citations in descending order. Then h is the number of leading papers whose citation count is at least their 1-based position.
Or avoid sorting: h can be at most n, so count papers into buckets 0 … n (counts above n go into bucket n).
Walk the buckets from n downward with a running total of papers; the first h where the total reaches h is the answer.

title: Sort Characters By Frequency
summary: Rearrange s so characters appear in decreasing order of frequency, each character's copies together. Any order among equally frequent characters is accepted.
statement:
Rearrange the characters of `s` so that they appear in decreasing order of frequency, with all copies of a character next to each other.

If several characters have the same frequency, they may appear in any order. Uppercase and lowercase letters are different characters.
constraints: `s` has English letters and digits only
hints: Sort the distinct characters by count descending, or put them in a max-heap keyed by count.
Bucket sort is O(n): bucket[c] holds the characters that appear c times. Walk the buckets from the highest count and repeat each character c times.

title: Maximum Gap
summary: Return the largest difference between neighbouring values once the array is sorted (0 if fewer than two values), in linear time and space.
statement:
Return the largest difference between two neighbouring elements of `nums` after sorting it. If the array has fewer than two elements, return `0`.

Your algorithm must run in linear time and use linear extra space, so a comparison sort is not the intended solution.
hints: With n numbers between min and max, the largest gap is at least (max − min) / (n − 1). So the answer never lies inside a bucket of that width.
Put the values into n − 1 buckets of that width, keeping only each bucket's minimum and maximum.
The answer is the largest difference between one non-empty bucket's minimum and the previous non-empty bucket's maximum. Radix sort is another linear approach.
